## Previously ...

Nine sessions. You have used an AI assistant in every one of them:

- To explain a concept you had just met
- To draft a consent banner and a privacy notice
- To write Tableau calculated fields
- To critique your own charts

. . .

Today we stop using it incidentally and name what is actually happening.

## Why Here

Block 3 is called "Python as the marketer's power tool".

. . .

In 2026, the power tool is not Python. It is **Python plus something that writes
Python**.

. . .

Pretending otherwise would teach you a version of the job that no longer exists.
Teaching it without teaching verification would be worse.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Distinguish chat, chat with context, and agentic use
- Choose the right mode for a given analytics task
- Verify AI-produced analysis rather than trusting it
- State what an agent must not be given access to, and why

# 1. Three Modes

## The Progression

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
**Chat**

You ask, it answers in words or code. It cannot see your data. You copy, paste
and run.

*The assistant knows things.*
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
**Chat with context**

You attach a file, a screenshot, an export. It answers about **your** data.

*The assistant knows your situation.*
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
**Agent**

It runs code, reads the result, notices the error, fixes it, and repeats until
done.

*The assistant does the work.*
:::
::::

. . .

Each mode is more capable than the last, and each removes one more of your
opportunities to notice that it is wrong.

## Mode 1: Chat

What you have mostly been doing.

> "What is the difference between a session and a user in GA4?"

> "Write a Tableau calculated field that groups source and medium into channels."

. . .

**Strengths**: fast, cheap, no setup, safe. It cannot damage anything because it
cannot touch anything.

. . .

**Limits**: it does not know your column names, your row counts, or that your
date field is stored as text.

## Mode 2: Chat With Context

You give it the situation.

> "Here is the first 20 rows of my GA4 export [attached]. The `date` column is
> reading as text. Write the pandas to fix it and tell me what to check
> afterwards."

. . .

**This is the single biggest upgrade available to you**, and most people never
make it. They keep asking generic questions and getting generic answers.

. . .

**Limits**: it sees a sample, not the dataset. It cannot run anything, so it
cannot know whether its answer worked.

## Mode 3: Agent

The assistant is given tools: a Python environment, a filesystem, sometimes a
browser.

. . .

You state a goal. It writes code, runs it, reads the traceback, corrects itself,
and continues.

> "Load ga4_export.csv, clean the date and numeric columns, and report sessions
> and conversion rate by channel and week. Tell me anything that looks wrong."

. . .

**This is genuinely different in kind.** The loop of run-observe-correct is the
one you will be doing by hand from next lecture onwards.

## One Model, Many Inputs and Outputs {.smaller}

![Source: [Masterclass: LLMs for Data Science](https://github.com/avvorstenbosch/Masterclass-LLMs-for-Data-Science) (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)](./figures/external/mcllm_multimodal_llm.png){fig-align="center" height="255px"}

*Text, image, audio in; text, image, audio out. The agent wraps a loop and a
set of tools around this.*


## What Makes an Agent an Agent

Three ingredients:

1. **Tools**: it can execute, not only emit text
2. **A loop**: it observes the result and acts again
3. **Some autonomy**: it decides the next step without asking you each time

. . .

Remove any one and you are back to chat.

. . .

The third ingredient is where the risk lives.

## Where You Will Meet Them

- **Notebook assistants**: Colab's Gemini, Copilot in Jupyter
- **Coding agents**: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex
- **Chat with code execution**: Claude and ChatGPT running Python on an uploaded file
- **Inside the platforms**: GA4's and Meta's own automated insights

. . .

For this module, **Claude** is the default in worked examples. ChatGPT and
GitHub Copilot do the same things with different names. The mode matters, the
brand does not.

# 2. The Spine of This Module

## One Step Per Block

<!-- Speaker notes: this slide is the reason the lecture exists here. Put it up
     again at the start of each block so students can see where they are. -->

| Block | Lectures | AI mode | What you use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Build the lab | 1-4 | Chat | A tutor. Ask it to explain, not to do |
| 2 See the data | 5-9 | Chat with context | Attach your export. Calculated fields, chart critique |
| 3 Python | 10-15 | Agentic coding | It writes and runs the analysis with you |
| 4 Metrics | 16-20 | An analyst you interrogate | Ask it to argue the other side |
| 5 Communication | 21-24 | A producer | Drafts the dashboard spec, the report, the deck |

. . .

Notice what is constant: **you own the judgement at every step.**

## The Direction of Travel

Each block hands more execution to the machine and keeps more verification with
you.

. . .

That is not a compromise. It is the actual job description of an analyst who
uses these tools well.

# 3. Verification

## The Only Skill That Matters

An AI assistant is a **confident** producer of plausible work.

. . .

Plausible and correct are different, and the gap is invisible from the output
alone.

. . .

Everything in this section is about closing that gap cheaply.

## The Four Checks

**1. Shape.** Did the number of rows change when it should not have? Is the
output the grain you asked for?

. . .

**2. Extremes.** Look at the largest and smallest values. Nonsense hides in the
tails, not in the head of the table.

. . .

**3. A known case.** Pick one channel or one week you can compute by hand or read
off GA4. Does it match?

. . .

**4. Reproduce.** Restart and run all. Then run it on last month's data.

## Verification Is Not Reading the Code

Reading the code catches syntax and obvious logic errors.

. . .

It does not catch:

- The right operation on the wrong column
- A join that silently dropped 40% of rows
- A filter that excluded exactly the cases you cared about
- A correct calculation of a metric that answers a different question

. . .

**Only checking the output against something you already know catches those.**

## The Failure Mode You Will Actually Have

<!-- Speaker notes: worth dwelling on. This is not hypothetical, it happens to
     every student who submits agent-assisted work. -->

You ask for conversion rate by channel. The agent produces a table. It looks
right. It is formatted nicely. You put it in your report.

. . .

It computed key events divided by **users**, not by **sessions**.

. . .

Every number is wrong by a consistent factor, the ranking happens to be
unchanged, and nothing about the output looks suspicious.

. . .

**The definition, not the code, was wrong.** No amount of reading the Python
would have caught it. Checking one channel against GA4 would have.

## Ask for the Assumptions

A cheap habit that catches a lot:

> "Before you write the code, list the assumptions you are making about the
> data and the metric definitions."

. . .

The assumptions are where the errors are, and they are much faster to read than
the code.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

Use an agent (Claude, ChatGPT with code execution, or Colab's assistant) on your
own GA4 export:

> "Load this export, clean it, and report sessions and key events by channel and
> by week. List your assumptions before you start."

Then, without looking at the code:

1. Check the total sessions against your GA4 report
2. Check one channel and one week by hand
3. Find the largest and smallest values and ask whether they make sense
4. Write down one assumption it made that you would have made differently

**20 minutes**

# 4. Limits, Cost and Safety

## What Agents Are Bad At

- **Small samples**: it will report a difference on n = 12 with no hesitation
- **Your context**: it does not know your consent decline rate or that you tested
  your own tags for a week
- **Domain definitions**: sessions, users, key events, engaged sessions. It will
  pick a plausible one
- **Saying "I do not know"**: it will produce an answer regardless

. . .

Every one of these is a thing you learned to worry about in Lectures 4, 6 and 8.
That is why this lecture is here and not in week one: you can now tell when the
answer is wrong.

## How Far They Can Actually Go {.smaller}

![Source: [MGT 100 Customer Analytics, UC San Diego](https://github.com/kennethcwilbur/mgt100) (CC BY 4.0)](./figures/external/mgt100_metr_three_fits.png){fig-align="center" height="320px"}

*Task length completed at 50% reliability, with three fits to the same data.
The disagreement after 2026 is the honest part of the picture.*


## What Not to Give an Agent

**Write access to your live GA4 property.** Configuration changes are not
reversible and historical data does not restate. Lectures 3 and 4 explained why.

. . .

**Your live site, unsupervised.** A broken tag costs you weeks of data.

. . .

**Personal data.** Your GA4 export is pseudonymous, but a comments dataset with
names in it is not. Lecture 4 applies to what you paste into a chat window.

. . .

**Client credentials.** Ever.

## Who Gains, Who Loses {.smaller}

![Source: [MGT 100 Customer Analytics, UC San Diego](https://github.com/kennethcwilbur/mgt100) (CC BY 4.0)](./figures/external/mgt100_genai_effects_table.png){fig-align="center" height="350px"}

*Most studies find generative AI narrows the gap between high and low
performers. A few find the opposite. Note which tasks are which.*


## Cost

Agents are not free, in money or in time.

. . .

A long agentic session on a small dataset can cost more than doing it yourself,
and a wrong answer you then have to debug costs far more.

. . .

**Rule of thumb**: chat for questions, context for one-off analysis, agents for
work you will repeat or work large enough that the loop pays for itself.

## Disclosure

For this module:

- **You may use AI for anything.** There is no penalty and no need to hide it.
- **You must say what you used it for.** One short section in your notebook or
  report: which tasks, which tool, what you changed.
- **You are responsible for every number you submit.** "The AI produced it" is
  not a defence, in this module or in a job.

. . .

This is the same principle as the measurement plan in Lecture 3, and the one the
cleaning log will formalise in Lecture 15. The reader must be able to tell what
you did.
